text: This is fairly typical epidote. The epidote is almost all of this field of
view. High relief, very high relief, not quite as high as the titanite, which are
the little brown grains in there. But what's distinctive other than the high
relief is when you cross the polars you get just a wide array of colors. It's
distinctive lemon yellow and this sort of anomalous royal blue color. But then
also really intense colors. I tell my students it's like magic markers.
Sometimes epidote is distinctly yellow or sort of a yellowish green in thin
section. That's what this epidote is. And again when you cross the polars you get
this really interesting array of interference colors. It's super intense.
I like this epidote because it has that really distinctive interference color. So
if you look at those those central grains, high relief, when you cross the
polars you get this lemon yellow and sort of sky blue to slightly darker blue
interference color. It's a little bit zoned, which is probably meaning that
it's chemically zoned, but that's really characteristic of epidote.
Most epidote that you see has a fairly high ferric iron content and that's one
of the reasons it has this intense interference colors or the blue and
yellow. But if there's a very low ferric iron content, so it's actually either
Kleinazoa site or Zoa site, the interference colors are gray. That's
what you're seeing here. It's very hard to tell the difference between Kleinazoa
site and orthorhombic Zoa site, but Kleinazoa site has very slightly inclined
extinction and Zoa site has parallel extinction. This is, I think, Zoa site.
You'll see that when the polars are crossed it has that same kind of gray
interference colors. There's a little bit of modeling to it and you typically see
that in these sorts of crystals. There's probably some chemical zoning and it
could be in lots of different things. It could be in ferric iron or rare earth
elements or something like that.
Alenite is a rare earth element epidote, so lanthanides plus scantium and
yttrium. Like all epidote group minerals has high relief here. It's actually just
the pleochroism brown core that's the alanite. And when I cross the polars
you'll see that the outer edge is this sort of slightly anomalous blue
interference color epidote. So it's just the core is alanite and the rim is
epidote. That's typically what you see in igneous alanites.
And then here is a metamorphic alanite. So that sort of cloudy core in that
central high relief grain is the alanite. When I cross the polars you'll see
the anomalous blue interference colors of the epidote that's around the
outside. So there you see it. In some metamorphic rocks the alanite just looks
like a little fuzzball and you have to go to high magnification to really
verify that it's alanite.
So here's a high magnification image of a metamorphic alanite. The alanite is
that brown pleochroism core, a little bit off-center of the higher leaf
grain. And then when I cross the polars you're going to see those really intense
magic marker type interference colors of the surrounding epidote.
I love this crystal. This is pymontite. Pymontite is a manganese bearing
epidote. And you can see there's actually epidote in here that has pymontite
that's grown over it on the rims. But this is an actual single crystal of
pymontite and it shows that distinctive pinkish to orange pleochroism.
And I couldn't resist. Here's epidote with pymontite over growths on it and you
can see that pink to orange pleochroism of pymontite while the epidote really
doesn't show much pleochroism at all. And then you can see the different
interference colors for the core of the epidote is similar to other sorts of
epidotes that we've looked at.
